extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, evolutionary biologists, and educated general readers interested in sexual selection and inheritance
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize Darwin's principles and empirical rules about sexual selection, the differing roles and variability of the sexes, and laws of inheritance (age-, season-, and sex-limited transmission).

rubrics_metrics.name: Male eagerness and female coyness in courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is, as far as I can discover, almost invariably the male which retains such organs, or has them most developed... The female, on the other hand, with the rarest exceptions, is less eager than the male. As ... Hunter long ago observed, she generally ‘requires to be courted;’ she is coy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues from broad observations across many classes that the male is usually the more active seeker in courtship while the female is comparatively passive but still exerts some choice, sometimes accepting the least distasteful male. Examples and citations are given throughout to support the generality of this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason why males typically seek the female (historical/functional explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because in plants and many affixed or lowly-organised aquatic animals the male element is brought to the female (pollen, antherozoids), descendants that became locomotive retained the habit of the male approaching the female.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses analogies to plants and sessile aquatic animals to explain why males of many free-living species approach females: transport constraints on gametes and ancestral habits can drive which sex becomes the seeker. He notes exceptions (e.g., species where females are fixed) and acknowledges some cases are difficult to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male eagerness leads to more frequent development of secondary sexual characters in males
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great eagerness of the males has thus indirectly led to their much more frequently developing secondary sexual characters than the females.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because more eager males that successfully obtain mates leave more offspring, sexual selection concentrates on males and favours the evolution of ornaments, weapons, and other secondary sexual traits. Darwin links eagerness, mating success, and accumulation of such traits over generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater variability of males
rubrics_metrics.description: Males are often more liable to vary than females — supported by studies of domesticated animals and human measurements showing greater range and frequency of abnormalities in males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites domesticated breeds, the Novara expedition measurements, and studies of muscles, supernumerary digits, ear-shape, and body temperature as evidence that males often show greater variability. He suggests this greater variability would facilitate the development of secondary sexual characters in males.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in expenditure and constitution between the sexes affecting variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The female expends much organic matter in forming ova, whereas the male expends force in contests, wandering, voice, secretions, etc.; this differing expenditure and timing (concentrated during breeding season) affects constitution and tendencies to vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin proposes that differing life-history investments (timing and type of expenditure) produce constitutional differences between sexes, which in turn influence how they vary (e.g., male vigour during the season intensifying colours independently of selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection is less rigorous than natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sexual selection acts in a less rigorous manner than natural selection. The latter produces its effects by the life or death at all ages of the more or less successful individuals... Generally the less successful male merely fails to obtain a female... so that they leave fewer, less vigorous, or no offspring.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin contrasts mechanisms: natural selection acts through survival across ages, sexual selection through differential mating success. Sexual selection can drive extreme modifications with no definite limit so long as variations arise, but natural selection will check traits that are highly injurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between transmission and development of characters (pangenesis hypothesis invoked)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two elements of 'inheritance' are distinguished—the transmission, and the development of characters; characters can be transmitted through both sexes but developed only in one. Darwin uses the hypothesis of pangenesis to explain gemmules transmitted to offspring that may remain dormant until proper conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes that some characters are transmitted even when not expressed immediately (e.g., secondary sexual traits present in both sexes' transmitted material but only developed in one sex). He illustrates with hybrids, castration, old age, and anomalous expression, and proposes pangenesis as a conceptual aid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance at corresponding periods of life (age-limited inheritance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new character appearing at a young age in a parent will generally reappear in the offspring at the same age; characters appearing at maturity or old age tend to reappear at the same advanced age in offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives examples from breeds of fowl and pigeons where plumage or other traits appear at particular moults or ages and are faithfully transmitted to offspring at the corresponding period. He notes exceptions and complications (e.g., anticipation or delay of expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance at corresponding seasons of the year
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters appearing periodically at different seasons (e.g., horns of the stag, winter fur, breeding plumage) tend to be inherited with the same seasonal periodicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites seasonal changes like stag horn cycles, Arctic fur changes, and birds acquiring breeding colours only during the season, and suggests such periodicity of expression is part of hereditary transmission, though direct evidence of inherited seasonal colour-change is less certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance as limited by sex (sex-limited inheritance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are commonly transmitted to whichever sex first exhibits them and then developed in that sex alone; equal transmission to both sexes is common when sexual differences are slight, but sex-limited transmission is frequent when sexual dimorphism is marked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include breeds of sheep and goats with horns differing by sex, tortoise-shell colouring in cats confined to females, and many fowl breeds where sex-specific characters are transmitted to the same sex. Darwin explains how domestication has produced a spectrum from great sexual dissimilarity to similarity depending on which variations were sex-limited in transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of producing sex-limited characters by selection unless variation is initially sex-limited
rubrics_metrics.description: If a desired variation is not originally limited to one sex, attempting to fix it by selecting only one sex is extremely difficult and may change both sexes; but if variations appear already limited to one sex, it is easy to make a breed characterised in that sex alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin discusses hypothetical and practical breeding scenarios (e.g., pigeon tinting, Belgian breed with males streaked black) and quotes a breeder (Tegetmeier) confirming the feasibility only when sex-limited variation is present from the start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule relating period of development and sex-limited transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Two general propositions: (1) Variations which first appear in either sex at a late period of life tend to be developed in that sex alone; (2) Variations which first appear early in life in either sex tend to be developed in both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin acknowledges these rules are not absolute but provides comparative evidence (especially the Deer family) to support them. He analyses horn development timing across species (reindeer vs other deer), antelopes, sheep, and cattle to illustrate how early vs late onset of a trait predicts whether it will be sex-limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical correlate: timing of development predicts sex-distribution of trait (examples from Cervidae and other groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: In species where a structure (e.g., horns) is developed late in life it is often confined to males; where it appears very early it commonly occurs in both sexes (reindeer horns appear within weeks in both sexes; horns in many deer appear months later only in males).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses multiple species comparisons and enquiries to naturalists (Cupples, Nilsson, Blyth, Canfield, etc.) to substantiate the timing–sex relationship. He also notes exceptions and intermediate cases (prong-horned antelope, merino sheep) and the variable fixation of horn presence under domestication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protuberances on bird skulls conform to the timing–sex rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. W. Marshall concluded that with bird species in which cranial protuberances are confined to males they are developed late in life; where common to both sexes they are developed early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites Marshall's work as further support for the general rule linking age/period of development with whether a character is sex-limited or shared.
